the Good Night button
Why ditch the cloud? #
The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks.
Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break:
Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it.
Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well.
Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it.
Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device.
Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban.
On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows).
A way in #
I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server.
Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one.
All that said, two major things have changed.
First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys.
Ian Carroll
@iangcarroll
For the next few days or weeks, anyone now has a root CA thanks to eMudhra. Time to have some fun with MiTMing unwilling devices!
10:15 AM · Oct 20, 2026
So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it.
The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes.
Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud.
Our man in the middle #

hn.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
hn.text:
Solving long-horizon tasks without any extra training
0 / 24 on target · step 0
Vanilla LeWM can be augmented to solve long-horizon physics tasks on out-of-distribution goals. This method uses transformations on a memory graph to generate on-the-fly subgoals without any additional training. Shown here are some of the hardest tasks it solved.
There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1]
The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.
The three parts of a JEPA world model.
This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2] , a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3] , a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.
A goal image from Push-T
The planner is given an image like this one and has to make the scene match it. The gray T is the block, the blue disc is the robot's pusher, and the green T is the goal position painted on the table. One detail in this image turned out to affect the success rate more than replacing the predictor with simulated physics.
The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning.
Success on 250 long-horizon tasks
78 %
Vanilla LeWM
learned predictor
≈
77 %
LeWM real physics
the simulator itself
That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.
Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.
1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart
Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.
So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.
250 long-horizon tasks, goal 75 steps away
LeWM, all 75 steps at once as published
22%
Exact physics, all 75 steps at once the simulator itself
42% +20
LeWM given a new subgoal every 25 steps same model, shorter hops
80% +58
0 25 50 75 100%
Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.
LeWM's planning horizon is about 25 steps
Plan all 75 steps at once ... one search, far goal 22%
A subgoal every 25 steps ... three short searches 80%
Chaining 25-step searches through subgoals keeps every search inside the range where LeWM is accurate.
This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.
Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.
The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.
2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump
LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.
This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of th

hn.title: AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
hn.text:
Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock
View image in fullscreen
Gödel’s work inspired Alan Turing and paved the way for the digital age. Photograph: Alfred Eisenstaedt/The LIFE Picture Collection/Shutterstock
‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
View image in fullscreen
Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive “I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Did you solve it? Gödel’s incompleteness theorem
Read more
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.
Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.
In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.
“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
skip past newsletter promotion
after newsletter promotion
View image in fullscreen
A microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced Study Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.
The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

hn.title: Show HN: Isometric SF – A pixel-art map of the SF Bay Area
hn.text: Technical Write-up: https://www.justinchavez.com/blog/isometric-sf-how/ Hi HN! Showcasing this fun project. I took 1300 square miles of the SF Bay Area from Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and transformed them into a cohesive pixel map. It's really fun to explore and stumble upon various famous landmarks like Apple Park, Palace of Fine Arts, or UC Berkeley. The technicals involve using Nano Banana 2 to train a Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 LoRA which is used to prototype the style and generation methods. For final map I used Qwen to train a Klein 4B LoRA which reproduced the style at 1/4 of the cost. More details in the blog post. Let me know what you think! I really enjoyed this process of fine-tuning smaller open source models. If I did the map with Nano Banana 2 it would have cost around 7k USD! Credit for the idea goes to Isometric NYC.

Learn about vigilant mode .
The big one in this release is federation: Lonewolf can now talk to other XMPP servers. We also added direct TLS and a handful of extensions that desktop clients rely on.
Lonewolf is still pre-1.0 and runs as a single node. Full XMPP compliance and clustering are on the roadmap .
What's new
Federation
Your users can now exchange messages, presence, IQs, and roster subscriptions with people on other XMPP servers. If a host has a certificate and a public DNS name, federation is on by default, with nothing extra to configure.
Lonewolf authenticates peers by certificate only. The other server needs a trusted certificate and SASL EXTERNAL support. We don't support Server Dialback.
When the other server supports it, both directions share a single connection ( XEP-0288 ). Servers also tell each other their stanza size and idle limits up front ( XEP-0478 ).
Federation checks certificate revocation lists published by the CA, fetched over plain HTTP. If a CRL can't be downloaded, the connection goes ahead anyway. You can turn downloads off with s2s.tls.fetch_crls = false , or point s2s.tls.crls_path at a local file to use only that.
Direct TLS
Clients and servers can now connect with TLS from the first byte ( XEP-0368 ), using new dedicated listeners. Outbound federation discovers both STARTTLS and direct TLS endpoints.
More for desktop clients
Private XML Storage ( XEP-0049 ) gives clients a place to keep private settings and legacy bookmarks.
Software Version ( XEP-0092 ) answers "what server is this?" queries. It doesn't reveal the operating system unless you turn that on.
Both are enabled by default.
Short-lived certificates
Use letsencrypt.certificate_profile to pick one of the profiles your CA advertises, including short-lived certificates. If you change the profile, Lonewolf renews early so the new one takes effect right away.
SCRAM-SHA-512 (opt-in)
You can now enable SCRAM-SHA-512 and SCRAM-SHA-512-PLUS. Be aware that they come from an expired Internet-Draft , not an RFC, and aren't registered with IANA.
Even if you leave SHA-512 login disabled, new accounts and password changes now store credentials that v0.2.0 can't read, so rolling back isn't straightforward.
See the standards reference for exactly what's supported and the configuration reference for every setting and its default.
Build from source
Grab Source code (tar.gz) or Source code (zip) below, extract it, and run:
cargo build --release --locked -p lonewolf -p lonewolfctl -p lonewolfbench
The benchmark tool is now called lonewolfbench instead of lonewolf-bench , so update any scripts that call it. All you need is a stable Rust toolchain and a system linker on Linux or macOS. The quick start walks you through setup.

hn.title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026 (1960)
Palmfrets, Minnesota guitarist's invention, strikes a new chord
hn.text:
Musician Ben Ranson reveals his "palmfrets" invention at Stella's in Fergus Falls on Oct. 28, 2026. Contributed / Ben Ranson
By
Mary Olson
November 12, 2026 at 9:30 AM
Listen
Comments
Share
Share this article
News Reporting
News Reporting
Based on facts, either observed and verified firsthand by the reporter, or reported and verified from knowledgeable sources.
The Trust Project
What is this?
FERGUS FALLS — The back room of Stella’s restaurant in Fergus Falls filled with people on Oct. 28, all there to see musician Ben Ranson play.
Ranson, who grew up in Sebeka, Minnesota, and currently lives in Sandstone, is a regular performer at venues across the region, including in Fergus Falls. But Oct. 28 was no ordinary gig. That night, Ranson revealed something he’d been working on for years.
ADVERTISEMENT
It wasn’t a new song or a clever guitar lick, it was an invention called “palmfrets” — something Ranson believes could change the way guitarists use their instrument. It allows players to play new bass lines or melodies using their palm, a special set of frets called palmfrets and a technique called palmfretting.
The invention
The idea for palmfrets came to Ranson over five years ago.
Ranson had already been doing musical experiments — even constructing organ-like foot pedals and learning the seven string guitar — all in a quest to get more notes out of the guitar, specifically more bass notes.
He said the reason behind the invention, initially, was entirely artistic. He wasn’t thinking much about developing a commercial product.
“That was not on my mind at all,” Ranson said. “And it wasn’t really until I made one that really worked that it sort of dawned on me like, oh, this is something that people are really going to want.”
Ranson made an early-stage version of the invention in his garage, and said that, at first, he didn't recognize the importance of what he had created. He set it aside and left it in a corner for awhile — years, even.
Eventually, he returned to his forgotten creation. It was then that he began to hear the music.
ADVERTISEMENT
He drafted his ideas and designs on paper, and enlisted the help of engineers. Together, they created new prototypes made from 3D printed plastic and laser-cut metal parts.
It was during that time when Ranson said something shifted.
“It hit me, like, I’ve really done it.”
Ranson knew the plastic and metal version was not practical, and only lasted a matter of weeks. But it worked, and from there, Ranson said the engineering became more serious.
Serious enough that Ranson applied for a patent, which he received on Oct. 6, 2026.
Ranson had an inkling that this was something special, and recalled the first time he started playing the guitar with a solid prototype.
“I was like, ‘I’m doing things that Chet Atkins never did,’” he joked. “I just had this sort of realization, like, other people are going to want to do this.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Fast forward to Oct. 28 in Fergus Falls, and Ranson’s invention is now in the hands of other guitar players.
Musician Ben Ranson demonstrates his "palmfrets" invention at the Fergus Falls Daily Journal on Oct. 30, 2026. Mary Olson / Fergus Falls Daily Journal
How it works
Using the pisiform bone — a small, pea-shaped bone in the wrist, near the bottom of the palm — players depress a string on the palmfret, an extra fret or set of frets near the wrist of the picking hand. The player can then use the thumb of their picking hand to pluck the string fretted by the pisiform bone.
This frees up the fretting hand — the hand which frets strings on the neck of the guitar — meaning the player can move up and down the fret board more freely, and fret other strings because the pisiform bone is doing some of the hard work.
“So if you want to, you can move (the fretting hand) anywhere you want, play any other notes that you want to play,” said Ranson.
Essentially, guitarists could play a bass line with their pisiform bone and play other melodies or chords that would have otherwise been, literally, out of reach.
Learning curve
Ranson had some rules when designing palmfrets.
“One of the basic principles in inventing it has been: if it interferes with the normal way that you would play the guitar, it’s no good,” he said.
ADVERTISEMENT
“So the basic principle is you have to keep all of the function of the guitar as people know it,” he explained. “It has to add, but it can’t take away. That’s the basic principle.”
Still, adding another element to the guitar introduces a learning curve, even for players as skilled as Ranson.
He gave proof of the learning curve by showing a callus on his pisofone bone — a callus reminiscent of the ones beginning guitarists get on their fingers when first learning to play — and compared his skill-level with the palmfrets to being a teenager playing in their first band and only knowing six songs.
“That is the stage I am at now, frankly.”
During the reveal, other guitar players tested out the palmfrets, taking turns passing around acoustic guitars, electric, and even the bass.
Darren Quam, a musician from Battle Lake, who was in attendance on Oct. 28, tried his hand — or palm — at the new invention.
“At first, you know, it took me a second to kind of understand how you could use it,” Quam said. “But then — especially when Ben had us come up and try it — then, you know, trying it with my own hands, I was like, okay, I see how this could be very useful in certain situations.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Quam also commented on the learning curve.
“It’s not a whole new instrument, but it’s a whole new way of playing.”
Despite the new way of playing, during the reveal show, Quam seemed to catch on quickly, with Ranson joking “we’re going to have to take this away from you.”
From a practical standpoint as a gigging musician, Quam thought the invention would be useful for solo players.
“I think it really is probably the most useful in like a solo situation where you’re playing and you can accompany yourself, especially with those lowe

CERN Built the Large Hadron Collider's Next-Gen Magnets
hn.text:
Energy Journal Watch News
How CERN Built the Large Hadron Collider’s Next-Gen Magnets
New materials and processes are behind the 11.3 tesla superconducting magnets
Michelle Hampson
10 Nov 2026
3 min read
CERN researchers have been developing and testing new superconducting Nb₃Sn magnet coils as part of the Large Hadron Collider’s ongoing upgrades.
Florence Elizabeth Thompson/CERN
This article is part of our exclusive IEEE Journal Watch series in partnership with IEEE Xplore.
CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) uses extremely strong magnets to collide particles at nearly the speed of light, breaking them up into smaller components for study. The LHC is already capable of slamming about 60 particles together 40 million times per second in a single experiment, which has led to some of the most important particle physics discoveries of the century.
But scientists at CERN are not stopping there. They are currently working on upgrading the LHC for upcoming experiments scheduled to begin after 2030. The new iteration of the particle collider, called the High-Luminosity LHC , will slam more particles together than before. (The phrase “high luminosity” refers to the increased number of particle collisions.) CERN’s goal is to achieve between 140 and 200 particle collisions 40 million times per second in each experiment in order to increase their chances of observing rare particles or phenomena. To succeed, the collider will need extremely compact and high-quality magnets.
In a study published 24 September in IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity , researchers outline their journey to manufacture these next-generation magnets for the LHC, which require new materials and manufacturing techniques.
Developing Nb₃Sn Superconducting Magnets
The collider’s current dipole magnets contain coils made of niobium and titanium (NbTi) and can achieve strengths of 8.3 tesla . That is about 166,000 times as strong as Earth’s magnetic field. However, this magnetic force is the upper limit of what NbTi coils can achieve. For the LHC’s new quadrupole magnets, scientists are creating coils made of niobium and tin (Nb₃Sn), which will yield just under 12 T.
Susana Izquierdo Bermúdez , a magnet engineer at CERN who leads a team of about 60 people, has been involved in the development of these magnets since 2012. Over the years, she has contributed to many different aspects of the project, including early winding tests, electromagnetic design, mechanical design, manufacturing, and testing.
Izquierdo Bermúdez notes that while NbTi is ductile and can be wound after the superconducting compound has been formed, Nb₃Sn is brittle and cannot tolerate the large strains involved in coil winding. For this reason, the magnets are produced using a process known as wind-and-react: The cable is first wound into its final coil geometry, and the Nb₃Sn superconducting phase is formed only afterwards through a high-temperature heat treatment.
To start, the team takes a 760-meter-long cable composed of strands of niobium and tin and wraps it around a center pole to form a coil about 7.2 meters long with a 150 millimeter aperture.
Once wound, the coil undergoes a controlled heat treatment in an inert atmosphere. The temperature is increased over time, plateauing at about 210 °C and then 400 °C before peaking at about 650 °C. During this process, which takes several days, the niobium and tin in the strands react to form the brittle Nb₃Sn superconducting phase.
“After reaction, the coil must be handled very carefully because excessive deformation could damage the brittle superconducting material,” Izquierdo Bermúdez explains.
The coils are then smoothed over with a liquid epoxy resin, which fills any internal voids, cracks, or gaps, and finally is cured into a rigid polymer.
In their study, Izquierdo Bermúdez and her colleagues outline their efforts to manufacture more than 120 coils for 4.5-meter-long magnets and more than 70 coils for 7.2-meter-long magnets for the LHC. Four coils are incorporated into each quadrupole magnet.
In total, the team produced 250 coils, 25 of which failed either due to human error or challenges in the manufacturing process that left the coils with subpar electrical or mechanical properties. Izquierdo Bermúdez says that even the smallest imperfection can compromise a coil. In one instance, a coil had to be discarded because a single metal particle trapped between the coil and one of its protective components was suspected of interfering with its performance.
In September, Izquierdo Bermúdez’s team finished running quality control tests on the 7.2-meter magnets for CERN, confirming they reached peak magnetic forces of 11.3 T. The magnets are functioning well, and the team is now working to manufacture back-ups.
Izquierdo Bermúdez says that it is a great honor and responsibility to be a part of this work, which has been a large team effort. “It has taken many years of work by a large international team, from conductor and magnet development through manufacturing, testing and final integration. Seeing the technology reach this stage is something we can all be very proud of,” she says.

hn.title: IceWM
hn.text:
IceWM is a window manager for the X Window System.
The goal of IceWM is speed, simplicity,
and not getting in the user’s way.
It comes with a taskbar with pager,
global and per-window keybindings
and a dynamic menu system.
Application windows can be managed by keyboard and mouse.
Windows can be iconified to the taskbar,
to the tray, to the desktop or be made hidden.
They are controllable by a quick switch
window (Alt+Tab) and in a window list.
A handful of configurable focus models are menu-selectable.
Setups with multiple monitors are supported by RandR and Xinerama.
IceWM is very configurable, themeable and well documented.
It includes an optional external background
wallpaper manager with transparency support,
a simple session manager and a system tray.
IceWM is available on popular Linux distributions like
Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, OpenSUSE, Gentoo, Slackware, CentOS,
antiX, NixOS and on most *BSDs.
Software
IceWM was created by Marko Maček in 1997 using C++.
It is now maintained at Github .
Releases
The latest released version is 4.1.0 (2026-08-06).
Features
Easy to use, simple and fast
Standards compliant →
Fully usable with keyboard
Alt+Tab window switching
Efficient resource usage
Task bar (optional)
Multiple workspaces
Fully documented →
A large number of themes →
Usable with GNOME and KDE environments
Regenerates menus when configuration changes
Support for sound effects →
Multiple focus modes
Manual placement of windows option
Autoraising of windows option
Tooltips
Configurable keybindings →
Supports DockApps in a container
Tabbed windows
Screenshots
The IceWM Screenshots Collection
Themes
IceWM is themeable .
The visual appearance of icewm can be changed by a theme,
which is a collection of settings and small images.
Over 450 themes can be downloaded from box-look.org .
Extra is a collection of 91 highlights. See icewm -i list .
Translations
IceWM is translated into three dozen languages.
To improve the translation for your language at Weblate,
first register an account either here or there ,
then update .
Documentation
IceWM man pages
IceWM Manual
Themes Howto
IceWM FAQ
Bug Tracking
Report your icewm bugs on Github .
Only report it once and give relevant details.
Install the latest release as follows
$ wget https://github.com/ice-wm/icewm/releases/download/4.1.0/icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ tar -x --lzip -vpf icewm-4.1.0.tar.lz
$ cd icewm-4.1.0
$ ./configure --prefix = /usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
Install from unreleased development source code
Gettext must be installed.
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure --prefix = /usr
$ make
$ sudo make install
If you have cmake, an alternative is:
$ git clone https://github.com/bbidulock/icewm
$ cd icewm
$ ./rebuild.sh -r --prefix = /usr
$ cd build
$ sudo make install
Install package dependencies
To install all package dependencies
in one go use the following script.
$ wget https://ice-wm.org/scripts/os-depends.sh
$ sudo bash -x ./os-depends.sh
Verify package dependencies by:
$ pkg-config --modversion x11 xext xcomposite xcursor xdamage xfixes xres xrender xrandr xinerama xft fontconfig sm ice sndfile alsa ao gio-2.0 gio-unix-2.0 gdk-pixbuf-xlib-2.0 imlib2 librsvg-2.0 xpm libpng libjpeg
# or simpler:
$ ./rebuild.sh -d

hn.title: Gnomon. Git for Postgres data, built for agents
hn.text:
Gnomon
Git for Postgres data, built for agents. Give an agent its own branch of your real database,
as nothing more than a connection string. See every field it changed, merge it into main when it's
right, and undo it if it wasn't.
Gnomon runs inside the Postgres you already have. One extension, no copies, no second database.
create extension gnomon;
select gnomon . track ( ' orders ' ); -- history starts now, no backfill
select gnomon . create_branch ( ' agent/refunds ' );
select gnomon . use ( ' agent/refunds ' );
-- Every query from here on runs on the branch
update orders set status = ' refunded ' where id = 4182 ;
select * from gnomon . diff ( ' agent/refunds ' ); -- every row and field it changed
select gnomon . merge ( ' agent/refunds ' ); -- three-way, type-aware, conflicts as rows
select gnomon . undo_merge ( 1 ); -- and back
Documentation: https://gnomon.bitsinfra.com/
Install: create extension gnomon on PostgreSQL 15-18, self-hosted or managed (RDS, Aurora,
Supabase). See Installation .
New here? The tutorial takes ten minutes.
A branch of production, in an instant
A branch reads everything from main and keeps only what it changes, so it opens instantly and
copies nothing, however big your database is. Give one to every agent run, every pull request and
every test.
Your application doesn't change. A branch is a connection string: point a session at it, and the
queries it already runs read and write the branch instead of main.
Where
How
A session
select gnomon.use('feature')
One transaction (behind a pooler)
select gnomon.begin('feature')
A connection string
gnomon branch url feature
With the C module
SET gnomon.branch = 'feature'
A past moment
select gnomon.use('main', '2026-10-31 23:59')
Schema changes come along too. Run a migration on a branch to add a column, rename one or create a
table, and main stays as it is until the merge, which brings the new shape and its data across
together.
Review data like code
Every branch comes with a diff: each row and field it changed, before and after. Review it in your
browser, comment on a single row and settle conflicts side by side. When an agent is done, Gnomon
opens the review and sends you the link.
Add checks written in SQL, and Gnomon runs them on the merged result before the merge is allowed to
land. An approval covers what you saw: if the branch changes afterwards, it comes back to you.
Merges that understand your data
When main and a branch change the same value, Gnomon doesn't just pick a side. Counts add up, JSON
merges key by key and text merges line by line. Anything that truly clashes becomes a conflict, for
a person to settle or for a query to resolve.
Branches merge into each other too, not only into main, and a single transaction can be picked from
one branch onto another. Undo works the same way: take back one transaction, everything an agent
did this afternoon, or a whole merge.
Any moment, exactly as it was
Gnomon keeps the history of every table you track. Read the whole database as it was at any moment,
with the queries you already have, and get the same answer every time. When an agent makes a
decision, you can see exactly what it saw.
-- The open invoices at the end of October
select gnomon . use ( ' main ' , ' 2026-10-31 23:59 ' );
select sum (amount) from invoices where status = ' open ' ;
The same history streams out as it happens, to Kafka, NATS or a webhook, and into dbt as snapshots
that keep deleted rows. Older history can move to object storage, and Gnomon brings it back when a
query reaches that far.
When a check that used to pass starts failing, gnomon bisect finds the transaction that broke it:
who made it, when and why.
Safe to hand to an agent
One command gives an agent a database role, a branch of its own and a connection string. That's all
it needs, whatever it's built with. It reads and writes its branch, and the database refuses the
rest, main included, even when the agent asks for it by name.
# A database role, a branch of its own and a connection string
gnomon agent create support-bot
It merges only what you allow. Merging is for the people you choose, or for an agent within
rules you write: at most twenty rows, only these tables, every check passing. Postgres enforces
them, whatever the agent is told.
Nothing leaves before you approve. Emails, webhooks and payments an agent queues stay on its
branch until the merge.
Every change has a name on it. Each change records the agent, the run and the reason it gave.
Replay what it saw. Gnomon records the moment of every read, so a replay returns exactly the
rows the agent read.
Try a few ways at once. Start several attempts from the same moment, compare their changes
and checks, and keep the best one.
Stop it, and take it back. One command locks an agent out, closes its branches and undoes
what it merged, newest first.
Ready for your agents. The Gnomon MCP server, on the agent's machine or over HTTP, lets it
explore the schema, try a change without keeping it, and rewind its branch to a checkpoint.
Build it into your product
The TypeScript and Python SDKs give each task your agents take on a run: a branch of its own, with
limits already set. Merge it, send it for review, or let it go.
import { Gnomon } from "@bitsinfra/gnomon" ;
import { nodePostgres } from "@bitsinfra/gnomon/pg" ;
const gnomon = new Gnomon ( {
app : nodePostgres ( appPool ) , // your application's own login
runs : nodePostgres ( runsPool ) , // one login shared by every agent run
} ) ;
// A branch for this task, discarded unless it's merged or submitted
await using run = await gnomon . startRun ( {
task : "Refund order 4182" ,
actor : "support-bot" ,
} ) ;
await run . sql ( "update orders set status = 'refunded' where id = 4182" ) ;
const { checks , changes } = await run . summary ( ) ;
if ( checks . passed && changes . rows <= 20 ) await run . merge ( ) ;
else await run . submit ( { title : "Refund order 4182" } ) ;
Runs can't read each other's branches, even when they share one dat

Concurrent Shell Command Queues
hn.text:
Concurrent Shell Command Queues
Christian Emmer
Nov 6, 2026* · 10 min read
How to run shell commands in parallel while limiting their concurrency.
I had a use case recently where I wanted to speed up some Bash processing that I was doing, but still keep concurrency constrained. So I wondered: is there a straightforward way to create thread pools in Bash? The answer is: yes, but it takes some work to be semi-resilient and portable.
You may ask: why do this in Bash at all? It seems silly to use a language with poor concurrency controls. You'd be right to ask this question, and my answer is: because I have a fondness for Bash , and I wanted the challenge. But you're still probably better off using another language, such as Python .
Here is code that creates a command queue that accepts shell commands to execute. You do not need to know all the commands that you want executed up-front, you can submit commands to it over time.
bash
1 # Start this shell's command queue.
2 # @param {number} $1 Maximum number of jobs to run at once
3 queue_start () {
4 # Validate that the parallelism is a valid limit for xargs
5 if [[ ! ${1:-} =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
6 echo "queue_start: size must be a positive integer, got ' ${1:-} '" >&2
7 return 1
8 fi
9
10 # Close this shell's copy (not the parent's) of an inherited or earlier
11 # command queue's file descriptor
12 if [[ -n ${_queue_fd:-} ]]; then
13 eval "exec ${_queue_fd} >&-"
14 unset _queue_fd _queue_pid
15 fi
16
17 # Find the first unused fd from 3 to 9 (zsh's redirect max)
18 local fd=3
19 while { : <& " ${fd} " ; } 2>/dev/null; do fd=$(( fd + 1 )); done
20 if [[ ${fd} -gt 9 ]]; then
21 echo "queue_start: no free fd from 3 to 9" >&2
22 return 1
23 fi
24
25 # Make a FIFO queue file in a private temporary directory
26 local dir
27 dir =$( mktemp -d " ${TMPDIR:-/tmp} /queue.XXXXXX" )
28 mkfifo " ${dir} /queue"
29
30 # Find the shell to execute commands (the current shell)
31 local shell
32 shell=$(ps -o comm = -p "$$" )
33 shell= ${shell#-}
34
35 # Start xargs in the background, reading NUL-separated commands from the
36 # queue file. Job messages are hidden by turning off job control and
37 # discarding the block's stderr. xargs gets the real stderr through a copy on
38 # the queue files's fd, until the file is opened.
39 eval "exec ${fd} >&2"
40 local opts=$-
41 set +m
42 {
43 # shellcheck disable=SC2016
44 xargs -0 -n 1 -P " $1 " " ${shell} " -c '
45 # Output is captured rather than streamed so that command output stays separate
46 out=$(eval -- "$1" </dev/null 2>&1); rc=$?
47 [ -z "${out}" ] || printf "%s\n" "${out}"
48 # Coerce non-zero exit codes to 1, because a 255 code would stop xargs
49 [ "${rc}" -eq 0 ] || { printf "exit %d: %s\n" "${rc}" "$1" >&2; exit 1;
50 }' _ < " ${dir} /queue" 2>& " ${fd} " &
51 _queue_pid=$!
52 disown || :
53 } 2>/dev/null
54 if [[ ${opts} == *m* ]]; then set -m; fi
55
56 # Open the queue file for writing, which waits until xargs has opened it for reading
57 # With both ends open, the file can be safely deleted
58 eval "exec ${fd} >\"\${dir}/queue\""
59 _queue_fd= ${fd}
60 rm -rf " ${dir} "
61
62 # Register an exit handler to terminate this PID's children, ensuring zsh behaves like bash
63 setopt localoptions posixtraps 2>/dev/null || :
64 trap _queue_stop EXIT
65 if [[ $- != *i* ]]; then
66 trap 'exit 129' HUP
67 trap 'exit 130' INT
68 trap 'exit 143' TERM
69 fi
70 }
71
72 # Queue a command on this shell's command queue.
73 # @param {string} $1 Command to run
74 queue_submit () {
75 if [[ -z ${_queue_fd:-} ]]; then
76 echo "queue_submit: no command queue started in this shell" >&2
77 return 1
78 fi
79 # Write the command to the queue file, blocking if it is full
80 # Use a printf process so that if xargs has exited, printf will get killed and not this shell
81 if [[ $- == *i* ]]; then
82 # Write the command in the foreground, because an interactive shell won't
83 # have any TERM/HUP/INT traps that could be delayed by a full queue
84 env printf '%s\0' " $1 " >& " ${_queue_fd} "
85 else
86 # Write the command in the background, so that a full queue doesn't delay any TERM/HUP/INT traps
87 env printf '%s\0' " $1 " >& " ${_queue_fd} " &
88 wait "$!"
89 fi || {
90 echo "queue_submit: couldn't queue the command; the command queue may have stopped" >&2
91 return 1
92 }
93 }
94
95 # Close the queue file so xargs finishes the jobs it has, then wait for it to exit
96 queue_wait () {
97 if [[ -z ${_queue_fd:-} ]]; then
98 echo "queue_wait: no command queue started in this shell" >&2
99 return 1
100 fi
101 eval "exec ${_queue_fd} >&-"
102 while kill -0 " ${_queue_pid} " 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.1; done
103 unset _queue_fd _queue_pid
104 }
105
106 # Stop every process below the given PID.
107 # @param {number=} $1 PID whose descendants to stop, defaulting to this shell's PID
108 _queue_stop () {
109 # Default to this shell's PID, found from a child's parent PID because $$ is
110 # the parent's PID in a subshell
111 local parent= ${1:-$(exec sh -c 'echo " ${PPID} "')}
112 local pid
113 for pid in $( exec pgrep -P " ${parent} " ); do
114 # Pause the process so it can't start any new children
115 kill -STOP " ${pid} " 2>/dev/null || continue
116 # Terminate the process' descendants, then terminate the process
117 _queue_stop " ${pid} "
118 kill -TERM " ${pid} " 2>/dev/null || :
119 # Resume the process so it can respond to the termination
120 kill -CONT " ${pid} " 2>/dev/null || :
121 done
122 }
123
124 # Stop all background processes on exit, because they ignore Ctrl-C and don't receive TERM
125 if [[ $- != *i* ]]; then
126 trap _queue_stop EXIT
127 trap 'exit 129' HUP
128 trap 'exit 130' INT
129 trap 'exit 143' TERM
130 fi
queue_start initializes the queue (managed by mkfifo ) and starts the executor (concurrency managed by xargs -P ), queue_submit submits commands to the queue, and queue_wait waits for the queue to drain before cleaning up. Calling queue_wait is optional, command processing will start as soon as you queue it with q

hn.title: Brave Search API now accepts agentic payments via the x402 protocol
hn.text:
The Brave Search API , our developer tool for building applications with data from the Web, is adding support for instant, pay-as-you-go, agentic payments enabled by the open x402 payment protocol. Developers and autonomous AI agents that specifically require agentic search can now programmatically query Brave’s independent search index, ground agent responses, and settle requests in real time, which eliminates the need for traditional API key management.
Integrating x402 with the Brave Search API makes it easier for an agentic harness to leverage Brave Search API via a CLI wallet, as Brave runs its own facilitator accepting USDC on the Base blockchain, with acceptance on other networks and with other stablecoins incoming soon. This allows a Brave Search API user the ability to pay for LLM Context (agentic grounding) or general web search on-demand, without first creating an account and selecting a plan. Instead, simply transfer USDC stablecoin to your agent’s wallet via the Base network and it’s ready to access the same high-quality search results powered by Brave’s search engine.
How does it work?
Brave Search API endpoints behind x402 require payment on every request rather than authentication. A request sent without payment receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response that states the price of that search and the payment details needed to pay it. The agent signs a USDC payment for that amount and retries the request with the signed payment attached. Once the payment is verified, the search runs and results are returned with a receipt of the transaction that occurred on the Base blockchain.
Get started today
Pricing follows Brave’s published API rates: LLM Context, an API designed specifically for providing search context for agents, will cost $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Additionally, web (search for humans), news, image, video, and local endpoints will also be available for $0.005 ($5 per 1,000). Gas fees for transacting on the Base blockchain will be covered for a limited time. Since each request carries its own payment, a Brave Search API account is no longer needed to use the service.
The easiest path to query via x402 is to install Purl Wallet, a Stripe-developed CLI wallet for your agent. Set up your wallet, top it off using Base-native USDC, and start querying today.
Ready to build pay-as-you-go search into your apps or AI agents? Check out our Brave Search x402 Proxy Documentation and explore: https://api-dashboard.search.brave.com/documentation/guides/agent-payments

hn.title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400M crypto hack, says FBI
hn.text:
North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google
Kelly Ng
FBI
FBI redacted examples of the 900 victim videos secretly recorded by North Korean hackers
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

hn.title: Switcher (2004)
hn.text:
Home | About Folklore | Quotes
The Original Macintosh:
104 of 125
Switcher
Author:
Andy Hertzfeld
Date:
October 1984
Characters:
Andy Hertzfeld, Neil Konzen, Bill Gates, Bud Tribble, Steve Jobs, Steve Capps, Charles Simonyi, Phil Goldman, Tom Petrie, Victor Bull, John Markoff, Burrell Smith, Guy Kawasaki
Topics:
Software Design, Technical, Compensation
Summary:
The Macintosh's first multi-tasking environment
The Switcher About Box
The first commercial product that I worked on after going on leave of absence from Apple in March 1984 (see Leave Of Absence ) was a low cost, high resolution scanner for the Macintosh called Thunderscan, that I created in collaboration with a tiny company named Thunderware (see Thunderscan ) . I started working on it in June 1984, and by early October, it was almost complete.
Tom Petrie, one of the two principals at Thunderware (the other was Victor Bull, who I worked with on the Silentype thermal printer (see What Hath Woz Wrought ) , the first project that I did for Apple), arranged a few demos for various computer magazines, to curry favorable reviews to promote the product. On October 11th, 1984, I drove with Tom to an office in Hillsborough, to demonstrate Thunderscan for Byte magazine.
The Byte reviewer was John Markoff, a technology scribe for the San Francisco Chronicle who was one of the best reporters covering the personal computer industry. Tom described Thunderscan while I set up the demo and started scanning. John asked a few questions, taking notes with his IBM PC, which was running a character-based text editor that I viewed with the typical pious disdain of a Macintosh purist. As I was answering one of his questions, the phone rang.
"Excuse me," he told us, as he pressed a key combination on his keyboard, his monitor screen instantly changing to a different program. He talked on the phone for a minute or two, occasionally typing, before he finished the conversation and pressed a key combination to switch back to his Thunderscan notes.
"What did you just do?," I asked John, curious about the software that he was running. "How did you switch to another application so quickly?"
"Oh, I'm running Memory Shift. Haven't you seen it?" John responded. "It's a DOS utility program that keeps multiple applications resident in memory, and allows you to switch between them quickly. I've been using it a lot lately." John typed the switch command a few times in rapid succession, to show me how fast it could do its thing.
"You know, I think I could do that for the Macintosh", I suddenly blurted out, before I even thought about it consciously.
The 512K Macintosh, with four times the memory of the original, had just started shipping a few weeks ago. I had considered trying to run multiple applications simultaneously on the 512K Mac, but I was stymied by low memory conflicts and other potential gotchas. But now, as I observed Memory Shift in action on John's PC, I suddenly saw a simple way to do it, which didn't seem to be too hard to implement.
"Yeah, that would be cool," John agreed. I continued with the Thunderscan demo, but it was hard for me to concentrate on it, because I couldn't stop thinking about application switching. There were a few intricate problems to solve, but it seemed eminently doable, and I thought it would be incredibly useful if I got it to work.
Tom Petrie noticed how excited I was about the new idea and, as he drove me home from the demo, he reminded me of my prior commitments, and made me promise that I would finish the alpha release of Thunderscan as soon as possible, before daring to start something new. We agreed on a list of a dozen or so tasks, which I thought I could accomplish within two weeks. Once the alpha release was completed, I could take a short hiatus, in order to work on application switching, before diving back into Thunderscan to finish the 1.0 release, due by the end of November.
During the next two weeks, I focused on polishing Thunderscan to get it ready for the alpha release, but I also spent idle moments pondering the design of the application switcher. One fundamental decision was whether or not to load all of the applications into a single heap, which would make optimal use of memory by minimizing fragmentation, or to allocate separate "heap zones" for each application. I decided to opt for separate heap zones to better isolate the applications, but I wasn't sure that was right.
There were lots of little problems to solve. The most crucial one was that the system software kept lots of application-specific global variables in low memory (see Mea Culpa ) , which needed to be swapped during context switching, so each application could maintain its own set of them. The hard part was coming up with the precise list of exactly what needed to be swapped; many of the variables were obvious, but some were quite subtle, and dependent on how applications were using them. I knew that my first cut wouldn't be perfect, but I was confident that I could debug the inevitable problems once I saw how the applications were actually failing.
A few days after starting the push to finish Thunderscan, I received an intriguing phone call from Jeff Harbers, the manager of Microsoft's Macintosh applications team. Jeff told me that Microsoft had a very strategic project that they needed for the Macintosh, and that they thought that I was the ideal person to implement it. He wouldn't tell me anything else over the phone, but he offered to fly me up to Seattle to discuss it in person. Even though I was right in the middle of trying to complete Thunderscan, I was intrigued enough to accept his offer to fly up to Seattle and visit with him the following Tuesday.
Jeff picked me up at the airport, and we drove to Microsoft's main building where we were joined by Neil Konzen, a talented 23 year old who was Microsoft's main systems programmer on the Macintosh. I knew Neil from his days as an early Apple II hobbyist, when we collaborated on adding fe

hn.title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
hn.text:
Listen − 1.0 x +
Seek
0:00 11:11
One evening last fall, a middle-aged couple, heads bent in conversation, approached the table where I sat signing books. “Go ahead,” the woman urged. Speaking softly, her husband explained that he had Parkinson’s disease. Although he hadn’t read my novel The Weight of Ink , it was his understanding that it featured a character with Parkinson’s who chose to die by assisted suicide rather than endure her decline. He had some objections.
I was horrified—not because I’d written something that offended him, but because I hadn’t. Helen Watt, the character with Parkinson’s in The Weight of Ink , does not, in fact, end her own life. I didn’t know for certain where his misunderstanding had originated, but I had a guess. Just a few weeks earlier, I’d asked ChatGPT a few questions about my novel; it responded to certain queries with this false rendition of Helen’s plotline. Ever since, I’d worried that the misrepresentation might somehow have a real-life impact. Now, it seemed, it had.
Any working writer can expect to be called out for their choices; critique is part of the terrain. As a novelist, I’ve been chided for details including a character’s self-defeating relationship decisions and an incorrect date for a 17th-century full moon. But that evening in late 2025 was the first time I’d been called to account for something I hadn’t actually written. And even as I explained to the couple before me that what they’d seen online was incorrect, I wondered: How many other people had been similarly misled?
The proliferation of artificial intelligence has raised new fears about the long-term viability of writers’ already tenuous profession, as the technology infiltrates prize-winning writing, scrapes books for learning material, and perhaps erodes readers’ attention spans. But alongside that upheaval, another subtler sort of destruction is under way. AI-enabled meddling is turning the reader-writer connection into a hall of fun-house mirrors, and threatening to break the trust that is essential to that bond.
In the Monty Python sketch “ Bookshop ,” a customer requests a progressively more absurd list of copycat Charles Dickens works. Does the shop have a copy of Knickerless Knickleby ? Or perhaps titles by one Charles Dikkens (“that’s Dikkens with two K ’s”)? The customer’s insistence on the legitimacy of these books gradually drives John Cleese’s bookshop-clerk character into a frenzy. What was delightfully preposterous decades ago is now uncomfortably familiar. With a blizzard of literary fakery overtaking the world of books, discerning what’s real requires vigilance on the part of readers.
Read: The worst thing about AI writing
In 2017, when I published The Weight of Ink , there was no other book by that title in the English language. This remained the case until the fall of 2025. Since then, at least five other novels with titles identical to mine have become available on Amazon, three of them published in the space of three weeks. Several other books with nearly identical titles also are listed for sale. I don’t know whether, or to what extent, AI was used in creating these books whose content otherwise seems to bear little or no resemblance to my novel; I found only one that contains an up-front disclaimer acknowledging AI authorship. But as Will Oremus noted in a recent Atlantic article , new-book releases on Amazon skyrocketed after 2022, around the time that AI models became widely accessible to the public. “That’s probably not because humans suddenly dedicated themselves en masse to the written word,” Oremus wrote. Similarly, it’s hard to believe that this profusion of Weight of Ink s is the result of an abrupt, hyperspecific surge of entirely human creativity.
In some ways, I felt lucky to have just my title copied; in late 2024, my friend the novelist Daphne Kalotay discovered that her author page on Amazon featured a brand-new novel that she hadn’t written. This book, which Kalotay described as “an AI hallucination based on descriptions of Russian Winter ,” her 2010 novel, had been paired with a title and cover from a completely unrelated book from decades earlier and was being sold under her name. “What was most unsettling,” Kalotay told me, “was how difficult it was to prove it was garbage.” In the end, the Authors Guild, an advocacy organization of which Kalotay is a member—and which has launched a certification program designed to distinguish human-authored books from those generated by AI—succeeded in getting Amazon to delete the book from her author page.
This sort of scam is now everywhere in publishing. Generating book-length texts using AI costs almost nothing, and Amazon lets individuals upload a maximum of six books a week, allowing for endless churn. Anyone selling AI-generated texts need only mislead a few customers per book—whether by using an existing work’s title or an author’s name—in order to turn a profit . “Amazon spends a lot of time and effort trying to prevent these books from getting posted,” Mary Rasenberger, the CEO of the Authors Guild, told me, “but it’s always a game of catch-up.”
The fakery cuts both ways: Writers are also being bombarded by AI-generated phishing attempts in the guise of emails from appreciative readers. Such emails are so pervasive that, like many of my peers, I now sometimes hesitate to even open my reader mail. Each of these notes begins personally, only to morph into an offer of paid marketing services. A recent example begins: “Dear Rachel, This feels scary to send, but I’m trusting my heart today.” The subsequent description of my work’s ostensible impact (“Your words found me at a time when I was quietly falling apart”) is followed by a pitch for a marketing plan to promote my novella, I Was Here . These promotion schemes are, of course, more fakery; the Authors Guild maintains a running list of such scams, in which writers who sign up see their money vanish .

Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
The Antigravity Team

Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with our strongest models for long-horizon tasks, including Gemini 4 Carbon, in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Selecting Orchestrator (Carbon) from the model selector in Google Antigravity.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.
Pairing Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Carbon with the Antigravity SDK for automated open-source issue triage and code generation.
Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier.
Using Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Google Antigravity to upgrade dependencies, refactor shared utilities, and generate accessible image alt text.
Getting started
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out as Orchestrator (Carbon) and Orchestrator (Argon) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and as Orchestrator (Argon) for paid Google AI Pro subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business .

hn.title: Dwarf planet candidate appears which takes roughly 280 years to orbit our sun
hn.text:
The new dwarf planet candidate, called 2026 ED138, orbits on a plane tiled nearly 25 degrees compared to our solar system's main planets, suggesting it was disturbed by gravitational interactions with Neptune.
NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor Image Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Orbit data provided by the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPCorb catalog), funded by NASA PDCO and the Tamkin Foundation. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC
Matthew Holman , a senior astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, was sifting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile when something odd caught his eye. Running a custom-made computer program, he and his colleague Kevin Napier had already spotted more than 2,000 little bright dots in the telescope data, corresponding to newly discovered small objects in the distant solar system. But this one was different: It seemed to be big.
Holman managed his expectations. After all, astronomers in the business of finding distant objects are used to disappointment. “We all have ‘found Mars’ … in terms of a false positive,” Holman tells Smithsonian magazine. They find a bright object that seems really big, then, with a closer look, learn that it’s nothing very remarkable after all. “We’re all really cautious when you see something that looks like it’s large.”
Still, this object grabbed Holman’s attention, so he tried to verify it with Napier and Rubin solar system lead scientist Mario Jurić . They found the celestial body in previous photos of the sky throughout the past decade, which helped them zero in on its orbital path—and the more historical data they found, the more confident they became.
“We know that it’s real,” Holman says. “Every time you look at the predicted location, there it is.” They even found it in photographic plates from 1937, stored in the Harvard plate stacks , he says.
The object, called 2026 ED138 , is 46 times farther from the sun than Earth is, and it takes 281.1 years to complete an orbit. Now, the central question is whether it’s big enough to be classified as a new dwarf planet, which would put it among the rare ranks of only five other objects in our solar system.
“This is incredibly exciting,” Paul Byrne , a planetary scientist at the Washington University in St. Louis who was not involved in the discovery, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “It heralds a new era of solar system and planetary science.”
2026 ED138 3D orbit
Watch on
Dwarf planets are smaller planets that orbit a star and have a nearly round shape, which happens naturally with objects above a certain size, as their gravitational force pulls evenly on all sides . But dwarf planets are not large enough for their gravity to clear their orbital paths of similar-size debris—the eight planets of our solar system, meanwhile, have achieved that feat. (Pluto’s designation was changed from planet to dwarf planet in 2006 for this reason—its orbit is littered with icy Kuiper Belt objects.)
Quick fact: Dynamic dwarf planet
Ceres, a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, may contain salty water that can percolate onto the surface in some regions.
ED138 is likely big enough to be round and, therefore, a dwarf planet—estimates for its size currently range from 370 miles to 930 miles across. But astronomers will have to confirm that measurement, and from the object’s brightness alone, that’s impossible. A highly reflective, smaller object, perhaps covered in gleaming ice caps, might appear just as bright as a less reflective, duller body that’s much larger.
Astronomers have two ways to get the required data. They could observe the world in infrared light, which reveals the thermal energy that it emits after being warmed by the sun. “From that you can figure out how big it is, because we know approximately what temperature it should have,” Holman says.
Alternatively, astronomers could watch the dwarf planet candidate pass in front of a star. If they know how much light comes from that star and how fast ED138 is moving, they can calculate the body’s size based on how long it obscures the light.
Holman says people are working on making those observations with telescopes such as the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). The dwarf planet candidate isn’t extremely easy to see at the moment, he adds, but “in the next few months it will be, and people will try.”
The Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in these images between March and June this year.
NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA Image Processing: M. Jurić (UW), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)
Right now, astronomers recognize five dwarf planets: Pluto , Eris , Makemake and Haumea in the distant Kuiper Belt, and Ceres in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Experts have long suspected that there could be more of these objects, but many of them could have highly elliptical orbits that keep them too far away for us to see most of the time. What we observe is potentially the “tip of the iceberg of a few that are in the close part of their orbit,” Holman says. “There must be a lot that we just haven’t yet detected.”
The discovery also hints at a relatively unexplored area of our solar system—the region that’s in front of the dense, starry core of the Milky Way from our perspective. It’s harder to pick out objects against all the background light in that zone, and ED138 has been traveling through it for the past 25 to 30 years, Holman notes. “There’s a swath on the sky where we really don’t have a good idea of what is there,” he adds.
What’s more, ED138 is in the southern hemisphere’s sky, and a lot of astronomical observations have focused on the northern hemisphere. But Rubin is poised to help change that: The new telescope, which has the world’s largest digital camera and captured its first images last year, is one of several observatories operating out of Chile’s Ataca

hn.title: Edge0-145B: Frontier AI Capabilities on Your Own Computer
hn.text:
Today, we're open-sourcing Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B , together with our unified inference framework and deployment tools. Edge0-145B is the world's first open-source on-device AI model with 145 billion parameters. It brings coding, reasoning, and agent capabilities that rival frontier cloud models to your own computer.
On-device AI has long forced a tradeoff between model capability and what the hardware can run. Larger models demand more memory, bandwidth, and power; smaller models can struggle with complex work. Moving that work to the cloud adds model-provider fees, data-handling constraints, and a dependence on connectivity.
This release addresses those constraints in four ways:
The constraint
What Edge0-145B makes possible
Large models are difficult to run on personal hardware.
A 145B model runs locally on a compatible laptop, with reported peak memory of 29GB and decoding above 80 tokens/s.
Small on-device models can fall short on demanding tasks.
Coding, reasoning, and instruction-following results are competitive with specific frontier cloud models, as the comparisons below show.
A useful assistant needs to finish work, not just answer questions.
The model plans, writes and runs code, debugs errors, and checks results visually for projects such as 3D scenes, games, hardware programs, and PCB designs.
Cloud workflows bring recurring fees, sensitive-data restrictions, and network dependence.
Local inference incurs no corresponding cloud-model token or API fees; data can stay on the computer, and core capabilities keep working offline. Hardware and electricity still cost money.
We're releasing the full stack so developers can reproduce the results, evaluate or fine-tune the models, and integrate them into their own products.
Get the model weights , explore the inference framework , or try the Edge0 App .
How We Make 100B+ Parameter AI Run on a Personal Computer
Edge0-145B Laptop Performance: Memory, Speed, and Power
Edge0-145B makes a 145-billion-parameter model usable on a personal laptop. A useful local model has to fit in memory, process prompts promptly, generate fast enough to use, and keep power consumption under control. It also needs to sustain longer tasks.
Requirement
Reported Edge0-145B result
What it enables
Memory
29GB peak memory
Runs on a compatible personal laptop, such as a MacBook Pro, without a server.
Prompt processing
1,100+ tokens/s prefill
Processes long prompts, including dozens of pages of code, before generation begins.
Generation
80+ tokens/s decode
Generates faster than a person reads.
Power
Approximately 120W typical power
Sustains operation without throttling in the reported setup.
Long tasks
128K–256K context
Maintains essentially the same speed on long inputs, supporting extended work.
Our earlier Edge0-35B phone release reported peak memory below 2.5GB. On an iPhone 18 Pro Max, Edge0-35B delivers 37+ tokens/s using approximately 2.5GB of memory. Edge0-145B has roughly four times as many parameters; its laptop comparison reports 80+ tokens/s and 28GB peak memory. These measurements apply to different models and hardware.
On-device model scale over time. The chart covers 67 open models of at least 1B parameters from 14 labs, intended for phones, laptops, and AI PCs. Same-size base, instruct, and reasoning variants count once; each line tracks a lab's largest model, including releases before July 2025. Filled points mark new highs and hollow points other releases. The scale is logarithmic below 40B and linear above it. Apple is excluded because its weights are not released. Sources: vendor announcements and model cards.
Why On-Device Models Have Stayed Small
Memory limits kept most on-device models below 10B parameters before September 2026. Apple Intelligence's on-device foundation model had approximately 3B parameters, while Google's Gemini Nano came in 1.8B and 3.25B versions. Even a 7B model could consume approximately 4GB of memory.
Larger models faced a memory wall. Model weights occupy storage and must be read during generation, competing for limited memory and bandwidth with the operating system and other apps. Even an aggressively compressed 35B model could need approximately 20GB of memory, far more than a phone could make available.
Compute, bandwidth, and power created competing constraints. Larger models offered more capability, but strained memory capacity, generation speed, and battery life. Making models smaller helped them fit, often at the cost of capability.
Privacy alone could not close that gap. Apple Intelligence protected user data, but Apple acknowledged that its on-device model was not designed for agentic applications requiring general world knowledge. The prevailing assumption was that on-device intelligence could not match the cloud.
Under the Hood of Edge0: Four Layers of Model and Inference Design
We designed Edge0-145B and its inference engine together to reduce the memory and data movement that make large models difficult to run locally. The design spans architecture, training, loading, and scheduling.
Architecture: share large matrices across sparse experts. Sharing matrices substantially reduces the weights that must be stored and moved while keeping the expert count unchanged. Each group of 64 experts shares two large matrices, while each expert retains a small set of parameters that captures its differences. Previously, every expert stored a complete set of matrices. Of the model's 145B total parameters, only approximately 10B participate in computation on each inference step.
Training: build for local execution from day one. We train the model in its on-device architecture from the outset, with deployment constraints built into its design. This avoids treating local deployment as a compression or pruning step after training a cloud model.
Loading: pipeline GPU memory, system memory, and SSD access. Reading and computation overlap across three storage tiers, avoiding serial waits. Frequently used “hot experts” remain
