hn.title: US test reactor cleared for operations
hn.text:
US test reactor cleared for operations
Thursday, 12 November 2026
Oklo's Groves Isotope Test Reactor has been cleared for unrestricted operations by the US Department of Energy.
(Image: Oklo)
The test reactor, near Lockhart in Caldwell County, Texas reached first criticality in August, less than a year after groundbreaking. It is one of 11 advanced reactor projects selected by the US Department of Energy (DOE) in August 2025 for the Nuclear Reactor Pilot Program, a programme aiming to expedite the testing of advanced reactor designs under a DOE authorisation pathway.
The DOE has now cleared the final operations hold point for the reactor - also known as Groves-1 - allowing the facility to advance into its research, testing, and training phase. This will help Oklo prepare the teams and systems needed to support the efficient delivery and operation of future nuclear projects, the company said. Operating experience from Groves-1 will directly inform Groves-2 Forge, Oklo's planned isotope production and processing pilot facility, which is part of the DOE's Nuclear Energy Launch Pad initiative to promote the rapid development and implementation of advanced nuclear technologies by private industry.
With Groves-1 now cleared for unrestricted operations, Oklo said it will test its capabilities relevant to future isotope reactors and the company's fast fission reactor, the Aurora powerhouse.
Groves-1 will serve as a key training and qualification platform for nuclear personnel at future reactor deployments, alongside further equipment testing, including continued evaluations of control rod drive mechanism performance and reliability. It will also enable criticality and reactivity benchmarking operations that support Oklo's isotope production capabilities, its engineering and design models, and potentially light water reactors and the large light water reactor fleet. The company says the resulting data could also help improve fuel performance and power output in small and large light water reactors.
"Taking Groves-1 from greenfield to criticality in less than a year was an important demonstration of what our team can accomplish," Oklo CEO and co-founder Jacob DeWitte said. "Now we're building on that experience by operating the reactor, testing new capabilities, and learning directly from the work. Those lessons can help us develop the people, systems, and processes needed as we advance additional isotope projects and Aurora powerhouses."
"DOE's Reactor Pilot Program reset the nuclear industry's expectations for how quickly we can move from advanced reactor design to demonstration while upholding best-in-class safety standards," Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Reactors Chimi Zacot said. "Successes like Groves-1's criticality are now paving the way for what comes next."
New reactor designs for commercial use in the USA are reviewed and approved by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), but under the Atomic Energy Act - the fundamental law governing civilian uses of nuclear materials and facilities in the USA - the DOE has the authority to approve reactor authorisations for research, development and demonstration. That authority is now being used to enable advanced reactor developers to certify, build and test prototype reactors that can inform full-scale commercial deployment under the Reactor Pilot Program pathway.
In response to executive orders issued in May 2025 that called for at least three prototype reactors to reach criticality by 4 July 2026, the DOE revamped its authorisation pathway to streamline the process.
In October, the NRC finalised a rule allowing applicants to use relevant analyses, test data and other information from DOE or Department of War (formerly the Department of Defense) reactor demonstration programmes to support commercial reactor licence applications. The rule is designed to make NRC reviews more efficient by allowing the agency to build on existing technical evidence while independently evaluating the safety of proposed commercial projects.

hn.title: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
The Dawn of the Data Intelligence Engineer
hn.text:
GO BACK TO BLOG
The dawn of the Data Intelligence Engineer
Sql AI
Nov 11, 2026 · 12 min read
BY Jordan Tigani
I asked Nick Ursa, our lead data engineer (and MotherDuck co-founder), how AI had changed his job. His answer: "This is the first time in my career with no backlog."
You'd think that would leave him with plenty of time on his hands, but he's busier than ever. While the backlog is gone, the answers still have to be right, and a human still has to decide how much quality control to do. Whereas once upon a time his job was to make sure the numbers he was computing were right, now his job is to make sure that the numbers that an LLM or agent comes up with are right.
That's a different job from working a ticket queue. At Data Outpost on November 4, I proposed a name for this new role: the Data Intelligence Engineer. I think it's now the emergent role on an AI-enabled data team, and I’d like to share why.
What a data team is for?
A data team has one job: enable the business to make good decisions. The faster they can make those decisions, based on a more accurate picture of what is happening, the better those decisions can be.
The hard part has been the route a question takes to become an answer. It moves like a relay. A marketing leader comes into work on Monday and notices that there was a spike in churn over the last week. Why did that happen? They file a ticket with the data team to investigate. An analyst picks up the ticket, and as they dig in, they realize some key data is not exported from one of the data sources. They file a ticket to ask a data engineer to look into it. That needs a change in one of the data pipelines, so the data engineer makes the change, tests it, runs the backfill, tests the backfill, and resolves the ticket. Then the ball is back in the court of the analyst, who can build the dashboard that was needed. By the time it ships, the marketing person can no longer remember why they asked in the first place. The churn rate recovered a couple of weeks later on its own.
This isn’t calling anyone out as not operating effectively or urgently; nobody in that relay did anything wrong. But every handoff means waiting, context is lost, and the half-life of the ability to effectively act on the answer to the question slowly decays.
As an aside, we should note that there was a whole generation of AI enabled tools that didn’t really help; the co-pilot era made some of the turnarounds faster, but the problem was that there were too many handoffs to be able to act quickly enough.
Something is different this time
Before December 2025, the case against AI for analytics was easy to make. LLMs wrote bad SQL. Business logic was unknowable. The sensible conclusion was that this was never going to work. In fact, I used to talk about how data teams were more or less exempt from the disruption that was happening in other areas of software.
Then, all of a sudden, the ground moved. New models got better at SQL. Business logic turned out to be something an agent can figure out with some helpful context. And agents went multi-turn, which means they don't have to get it right the first time. They can try a query, look at what came back, and try again, just like a human analyst would do. Put those together and it … just … works.
Self-service BI has been right around the corner for decades, what makes this different? Well, as a bit of an existence proof, here’s an example; the presentation I gave at Data Outpost was not created as a powerpoint deck or Google Slides, it was an app that I built using MotherDuck and Claude . I used live datasets from four different data sources, built a number of interactive and animated visualizations. Anything I did could be done by virtually anyone; I didn’t look at a single line of code or SQL.
It is important to stress that this isn’t just a way to automate building your dashboards. BI is typically pretty static, with maybe a couple of drill-downs. But with AI, you can build much richer visualizations. And what’s more, if you can build a dashboard with a prompt, you can go beyond that and also build a full-blown app.
Allowing business stakeholders to answer questions with data on their own has an even broader benefit than just shortening the data team’s backlog; it actually allows them to make better decisions. By cutting down the amount of time it takes and the number of handoffs involved, they can ask more questions. They can ask follow up questions while they still have all of the context in their heads. This means they can make confident decisions faster.
Which of these jobs can be a prompt?
AI is dramatically changing the job information workers perform. Software engineers often find their time being spent babysitting Claude sessions and rubber stamping agent-written code. What about the traditional roles of the data team? Which of their jobs, to put it a bit provocatively, can be a prompt?
As uncomfortable as the answer might be, rather a lot can be done via a prompt. In the not too distant future, writing SQL queries, creating dashboards, and building dbt pipelines are not going to be things that require specialized knowledge to do. Agents are likely better than humans at these tasks already, and they’re only going to get better. Our Data Engineer, Nick, moved us from one version of Airflow to another in a weekend, with minimal supervision, which once would have taken a week.
Writing code or SQL or building dashboards was never the whole job, though. The need for accurate data and the ability to understand it doesn’t go away. And someone has to be accountable, who can sign off and say “yes, this is right”. That takes a human in the loop. Quoth Nick, one more time, “Data eng, regardless of tooling or who does it, is an accountability function."
What still needs a human
Once agents are writing the code, what’s left in the data world? It turns out quite a lot. Humans need to make sure that other stakeholders without the word “Data” in their title are

Get started with the Foundation Models framework
The Foundation Models framework is the best way to use any large language model in your app. Whether you’re generating a quick summary or creating dynamic agents, the framework has what you need.
Overview
The Foundation Models framework is a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into your app — including direct access to the Apple Foundation Models on-device and in Private Cloud Compute. Powerful capabilities like guided generation, tool calling, image understanding, and Dynamic Profiles are built in, so you have what you need to build unique experiences.
What’s new in the Foundation Models framework
Meet the Foundation Models framework
Foundation Models framework
Human Interface Guidelines for Generative AI
Image understanding
Multimodal prompts let you pass images alongside text so your app can reason about visual content. This opens up new categories of experiences you can build with image understanding — it's as simple as attaching an image to your prompt. The Vision framework is also integrated directly, giving your model purpose-built tools like OCR for precise text extraction and barcode readers for quick code scanning — all on-device.
What’s new in image understanding
Model support
The Foundation Models framework gives you direct access to the on-device foundation model at the core of Apple Intelligence so you can build experiences that are smart, private, and work without internet connectivity.
On-device models are highly useful for many tasks, yet sometimes you need a larger model for a more complex workflow. The Foundation Models framework now extends to server models — like Claude, Gemini, and more — all through the same Swift API, with full support for features like tool calling and guided generation. Any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol , a fundamental component of the framework that allows you to pick the right language model for your app.
Supported third-party models

Private Cloud Compute

Learn more about Private Cloud Compute
Build with the new Apple Foundation Model on Private Cloud Compute
Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework
Dynamic Profiles
Dynamic Profiles are new declarative APIs for continuously updating your session's model, tools, and instructions on the fly. Rather than creating a session with a fixed configuration, you define profiles — each with its own model, temperature, reasoning level, and toolset — and swap between them within a single continuous session. The session transcript is shared across every profile switch, so your app gets more contextual intelligence with less prompting. Dynamic Profiles are designed to be adaptable building blocks: use them to build AI agents, skills, or any other high-level abstraction your app needs.

hn.title: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots
hn.text:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.
The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.
OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.
The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.
Recommended Video
OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.
OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027.
The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world.
The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.
Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks.
Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute who had previously heard about OpenAI’s reorganization, told Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.
OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.
But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models.
The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.
This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.
But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.
Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

Turning a 22-year-old Postgres type-confusion primitive into RCE
hn.text:
If you had told me in April 2026 one question “Mehmet, can we use managed PostgreSQL for this project?” would send me into the deepest rabbit hole of my life, I would have laughed.
Months later, I finally found the bottom of that rabbit hole. It was a 22-year-old zero-day in PostgreSQL core.
In this blog post you will read a story of how I ended up uncovering a new class of type-confusion vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL.
This is the 3rd part of blog post series named “ Systemic Risks in the Managed PostgreSQL Industry ”. For those who have missed the first two part, feel free to start from 1st and 2nd which will give you a complete context of this madness.
TLDR:
I gave PostgreSQL a value inside a composite type, changed the type of one of its fields, and asked it to read the value back. That type confusion led to one of the most reliable memory-corruption exploit I have seen. But I did not start by looking for a PostgreSQL core vulnerability.
I was exploiting pg_clickhouse, and getting that exploit to work left me with a question about how PostgreSQL understands its own data. With an AI agent as my teacher, I worked through the internals one question at a time. Then a seemingly unrelated conversation gave me the idea that connected it all, and eventually I found myself staring at a primitive that had been there for for awhile.
This is the full true story of how those pieces came together, I am sure you will enjoy this story.
Beginning of August 2026
During June and July, I had been exploiting memory-corruption vulnerabilities across several PostgreSQL extensions. One of the extensions that I achieved code execution was pg_clickhouse . That case study has its own story, which I will share in the future.
What matters here is what that exploit forced me to learn. pg_clickhouse translates ClickHouse values into native PostgreSQL values. A ClickHouse Array is not a PostgreSQL array, right ? So the extension had to rebuild its elements as Datum values in the format that PostgreSQL expected. A mistake in that conversion was what eventually gave me a code execution.
This was my first time meeting with things like Datum , OIDs etc in the PostgreSQL universe. I learned only enough to finish the exploit, but one question remained in the back of my mind:
How does PostgreSQL itself decide what a value is? And how does it process and represent it?
Somewhere around late July, I finally got my head out of the extensions and just followed that question into PostgreSQL core.
Disclaimer: I reported pg_clickhouse oob write + read chain to the vendor and they fixed it at Jun 23.
PostgreSQL Types 101
I started learning with a very simple query. What happens when I run the simplest query SELECT 1337?
While I avoided all the black magic in Postgres internals, I kept this crash course on the basics of data types.
I start with this query.
SET debug_print_parse = on;
SELECT 1337; SET debug_print_parse = on ;
SELECT 1337 ;
The database scanner looks at the query, recognises SELECT as a keyword, and 1337 as an integer token. Then it creates a parse tree for the query. Next, PostgreSQL walks the tree and transforms it into a typed query tree.
{QUERY
:commandType 1
:targetList (
{TARGETENTRY
:expr
{CONST
:consttype 23
:consttypmod -1
:constlen 4
:constbyval true
:constisnull false
:location 7
:constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]
}
}
)
} { QUERY
: commandType 1
:targetList (
{ TARGETENTRY
: expr
{ CONST
: consttype 23
:consttypmod -1
:constlen 4
:constbyval true
:constisnull false
:location 7
:constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ]
}
}
)
}
Parse tree looks like above. But I just wanted to better understand things like what is the consttype 23 ? why constvalue has [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] and where is my 1337 value ? At this point, I asked Opus 5 to prepare me a full deep-dive course on PostgreSQL types. Spending a few days around there and talking with my agent, whom I named pg_expert taught me these:
consttype = 23 → int4
constlen = 4 → four-byte payload
constbyval = true → stored by value
constisnull = false → this is not NULL consttype = 23 → int4
constlen = 4 → four - byte payload
constbyval = true → stored by value
constisnull = false → this is not NULL
constvalue 4 [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] can be converted to hexadecimal, making the value easier to recognize:
57 decimal = 0x39
5 decimal = 0x05 57 decimal = 0x39
5 decimal = 0x05
On my little-endian system, the bytes were stored least-significant first:
39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337 39 05 00 00 → 0x00000539 → 1337
So 1337 had not disappeared. But why do we even have 8 bytes [ 57 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 ] instead of simply 4 bytes ?
That was because constvalue was not declared as an int32 . It was declared as a Datum , which was 8 bytes Our value 1337::int4 value stored at the lower four bytes of that generic carrier.
How can that same 8-byte Datum represent a text , an array , or custom types ?
A Datum Does Not Know What It Is
Chatting with my pg_expert agent taught me more. A Datum does NOT know what it represents.
The eight bytes carrying 1337 did not contain a hidden label saying “I am an integer.”. PostgreSQL knew its type only because of this consttype = 23 .
That number is an OID (Object IDentifiers) pointing to a row in the pg_type system catalog
SELECT
oid,
typname,
typlen,
typbyval,
typalign,
typinput::regproc,
typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid = 23;
oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput
-----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+-----------
23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out SELECT
oid,
typname,
typlen,
typbyval,
typalign,
typinput::regproc,
typoutput::regproc
FROM pg_type
WHERE oid = 23 ;
oid | typname | typlen | typbyval | typalign | typinput | typoutput
-----+---------+--------+----------+----------+----------+-----------
23 | int4 | 4 | t | i | int4in | int4out
That means the pg_type row shows what the value means and how PostgreSQL will use it. So far, it’s brilliant and easy to understand. But what about the text ty

Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
hn.text:
NPR >
K-12 Education
Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
By Sequoia Carrillo
Friday, November 13, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
Many parents do not.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."
Related Story: NPR
When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens , first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom .
But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified , Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.
In a post on X , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.
A baffling move
Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.
Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.
"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."
When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement , where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
The "AI or nothing" approach
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.
Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an " unacceptable risk " rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.
The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
Related Story: NPR
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.
Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.
Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen
Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

hn.title: The 42-Year Journey to Bring 'Neuromancer' to the Screen
hn.text:
Save this story
Save this story
Briana Middleton has something to show me. “Wait!” she says just as we’re about to end our Zoom call, reaching for something just beyond her screen.
“When I found out we were going to be doing this,” she says, “I was at the thrift shop in my neighborhood and I found this .” Then she points it at the camera: an issue of WIRED from 1995 featuring Keanu Reeves on the cover alongside the line “ William Gibson on the making of Johnny Mnemonic .”
Very apropos. The 1995 film Johnny Mnemonic was based on a short story by Gibson, who also wrote the screenplay. Molly, the “razorgirl” Middleton plays in Apple TV’s forthcoming Neuromancer adaptation, made her first appearance in that short story. Her relationship with the protagonist Case, played in the series by Callum Turner, mirrors the one Reeves’ Neo had with Trinity in The Matrix , which is steeped in Gibsoneque lore.
For Middleton, to be giving an interview to WIRED about Neuromancer ’s epic journey to the screen not long after finding a 1995 issue of the magazine in a secondhand store is so uncanny it almost feels like a glitch. “Dude, it was eight bucks,” she says, agreeing that eight dollars is a steal for a vintage WIRED. “I was like, ‘This is crazy.’”
Maybe all things happen exactly when they’re supposed to. Gibson originally released Neuromancer in 1984, back before hackers were cool. Back before hackers were CEOs. It focused on Case, a young computer jockey who can get online through a jack in his head. He teams up with Molly and a former military man named Armitage to break into the offworld home of the Tessier-Ashpool family, who became astoundingly rich thanks to the tech company they founded.
The book’s novel ideas—cyberspace, brain-computer interfaces, all-powerful AIs—were years away from being mainstream, let alone possible. In the years since, there’s been much talk of turning Neuromancer into a movie or TV show, but it never took off, even as Hollywood mined sci-fi for hits.
On January 22, all of that will change when Apple TV releases its long-anticipated adaptation . Ahead of its release, WIRED got in touch with Middleton, Turner, and showrunners Graham Roland and JD Dillard to find out how they became the first to bring the book to screens—and the burden of taking on one of sci-fi’s classics.
On adapting an iconic sci-fi novel:
Graham Roland: It's a huge seminal book. I had not read it until the summer of 2020, but I was aware it was one of those white whales. It inspired a lot of things, and people had been trying to adapt it for years.
Callum Turner: The world will be taken on a wild ride. It’s an epic. It’s Blade Runner ; it’s 2001: A Space Odyssey ; it’s The Fifth Element . This is the first time it comes onto our screens, and that's a big moment for us and fans of sci-fi.
Callum Turner as Case.
Photograph: Courtesy of Apple
Briana Middleton: When we were shooting it and in the thick of it, it was easier to not get freaked out by the expectations. It felt nice to be in a little bubble with the world that we had created. I tried to look at the expectations that people clearly have and the love that people have for this book and what these characters mean. I definitely get freaked out sometimes and I just have to shut my computer and not think about it.
On getting the rights:
Roland: I had a meeting at Skydance, and they had given me the book and said, “Hey, the rights of this book are going to come available again. We’re going to try to adapt it as a TV show as opposed to a movie or several movies." It made so much sense. So I read the book, and really responded to it right away. JD and I had been friends for years prior to that, and were looking for a way to work together. He had also had a meeting at Skydance, and they had also given him the book.
JD Dillard: Yeah, there was a wonderful kismet of this moment, and we were like, “Wait, we’re both talking to people about this. Why don’t we do it together?”
On how Drake became a producer:
Dillard: Drake has always been a fan of Neuromancer and as a storyteller has great taste, but that's only part of it. The real magic is that he’s built an incredible team at [his production company] DreamCrew that he trusts to bring things to life once he identifies something he loves or believes in. Jason Shrier, who leads film and TV for DreamCrew, is one of the folks in our little brain trust on this show, and someone we pride as always having his finger on the pulse. But he has a relationship with [entertainment company] Anonymous Content, and Skydance, so it was kind of serendipitous that as Drake and DreamCrew had identified the books, all of these parties were starting to form and realize that they could work together to go get the rights. Drake, individually and by way of DreamCrew, is part of the mix and remains an important part of our process.
On working with William Gibson:
Roland: The way it was set up was that William Gibson was going to be the decider of who was going to get the rights when they came available. So we went to work on a pitch and with the hope that we would be the people he would choose.
We had heard that there were some bigger names, much bigger than JD and I. I just felt like there was a counterculture vibe about him and I was like, I don't think it matters that we're nobodies. I think if we can somehow communicate our passion for his book, and not just go and say, “Oh, obviously we’ll take care of your book, you can trust us,” but actually go in and do the work and come up with a thoughtful presentation and a thoughtful pitch, then I think we've got as good a shot as any.

hn.title: Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth
hn.text:
Talking Zen 6 with Mike Clark at AMD In-Depth
George Cozma
Nov 11, 2026
22
5
Share
Hello you fine Internet folks,
I sat down with AMD’s Mike Clark to talk about Zen 6, the evolution from Zen 5 and what some of the differences are between Zen 6 and Zen 6c and what drove some of those changes.
Hope y’all enjoy!
The transcript below has been edited for readability and conciseness.
George Cozma: Hello, you fine Internet folks. We’re here at AMD In-Depth, where we’re talking about Venice. With me, I have a returning guest, Mike Clark. Would you like to tell the audience who you are?
Mike Clark: Hi, I’m Mike Clark, the original architect of Zen. Some people refer to me as “Zen Daddy.” I’ve been working on cores here at AMD for 33 years, and we’ve got another great one coming, so I’m very proud of the design team I get to represent here today.
George Cozma: I’ve had some hands-on time with Zen 6c. Let’s talk about the change that’s happened with Zen 6 and Zen 6c, what I refer to in my piece as the Zen 6 family. Why is it different from previous generations?
Mike Clark: Right. Starting with Zen 4, we’ve been going through this evolution of having two core families. Before, we were really just using the denser technology as an area play. In this generation, having learned a lot, as we were filling out that denser version of the core, we wanted to leverage it to add some extra IPC within the core. So if you look more in-depth at what we have, what used to be our classic design, we now think of as our high-frequency design. And our dense technology is now our top-of-the-line, no-questions-asked performance core, because we’ve also enabled the full L3 in that implementation, at 4MB per core. So we have 32 of those cores, 128MB of L3, and the highest IPC you can get in that core.
George Cozma: Awesome. So far, one thing I’ve noticed is that the vector scheduler is a bit bigger on Zen 6c. What was the reasoning for increasing that on Zen 6c?
Mike Clark: Well, that wasn’t the only thing we increased. One principle we follow is that we don’t want to create a delta between the two architectures that software has to be optimized for. We want them to have the same fit and feel, so the same optimizations apply to both. But because of its reduced frequency target, Zen 6c can have a little more capacity in the queues, since it doesn’t have to reach the maximum frequency the high-frequency core has to hit. The floating-point scheduler is just one example. There are other queues throughout the core that are larger in Zen 6c, to pull out a little more IPC and get a little more leverage in that SMT environment as well.
George Cozma: Interesting. Both Zen 6 and Zen 6c build on the design you had in Zen 5, and one of the interesting things with Zen 5 was the dual decode setup. Has the front end changed much to let a single thread make better use of both decode clusters?
Mike Clark: Yes. As you said, Zen 5 was a new foundation, with the ability to fetch two basic blocks and get them down the line. But it gets quite complicated with one thread running larger-footprint workloads, where some of it might be hitting the I-cache and some of it might be hitting the op cache, and you’re trying to get everything synced up. So we spent a lot of time optimizing that and making it more efficient from both a delivery and a power perspective: less power wasted, and more efficient delivery from that new front end.
George Cozma: Awesome. Going down into the execution engine, I also noticed that the number of integer multiply units has gone down from three to two. Could you talk a bit about what drove that choice?
Mike Clark: It really came out of the Zen 5 design, where we had a more unified scheduler. To make a scheduler simpler, you want the units it schedules into to be very uniform, and the way we had set up those schedulers, adding a third multiplier to the group it was scheduling into was easy and didn’t add complication. In Zen 6, we realized that to really scale out the architecture, we needed to go back to more distributed schedulers, which now schedule into the ALUs. We hadn’t seen much uptick from that extra multiplier on Zen 5, so to optimize the area and the schedulers, we went back to two multipliers.
George Cozma: Speaking of integer multiply, on the vector side you’ve added two more VNNI units. What was the impetus for adding them, and at what point in the design did you add them?
Mike Clark: As I said in the talk, these are long design programs. We weren’t designing Zen 6 to be an agentic core. When we started, no one was really even using that term. But Zen 5 was a whole new foundation for AI workloads, and we’ve always believed the core has a place in AI: orchestration, data type manipulation, smaller models. So we were always focused on making the core good at AI. It’s not going to beat a GPU, and that’s not the point. We realized we probably should have some more VNNI, given where we were seeing inference go, and the team rallied around that. It was kind of late, since these are long-lead projects and the floor plan was set, but the team rallied, we were able to squeeze a couple more VNNI pipes in there, and it was a big success.
George Cozma: Again on the vector side, one of the oddities of Zen 5 was that although the wires were all there, the load unit could only do two vector loads at a time. What changed within the Zen 6 core to allow four vector loads, assuming they’re either 128 or 256 bits?
Mike Clark: We can do the 256-bit loads. Since we were able to do two 512-bit loads, we already had 1,024 wires headed over there. Obviously, using them piecemeal versus as one contiguous set complicates the design. I think it’s something we always wanted to do on Zen 5, but with all the change and getting it working, we left that for the Zen 6 team, and they were awesome. We’re all really one team at AMD anyway, and sometimes things intersect at different points in the roadmap. This was the time to do it.
George Cozm

hn.title: Sift: LSP, Lint, Format Lisp, Scheme and Emacs Lisp
hn.text:
sift
an idempotent formatter, a rule-based linter and a language server for Scheme, Emacs Lisp and Common Lisp
sift reads a Lisp source file, reports what is ill-formed in it, and rewrites
its whitespace. The rewrite is a total function on text and a fixed point:
formatting a formatted file returns it unchanged, and a comment, a blank line,
a #; datum comment or a #. read-time form appears in the output in the place
it was in the input. Both properties are asserted over every fixture in the
suite, so neither is a promise that expires quietly.
Three dialects are read, each by the rules of its own report rather than by a
compromise between them: Scheme, Emacs Lisp and Common Lisp. A square bracket
is a vector in one of them and a clause in the next, and sift does not average
the two.
Install it with guix install sift or nix run , or clone the
repository and run ./bin/sift version . The implementation is Guile 3.0 and
the standard library, with no C dependency and no build step, because a Scheme
program has none; sift doctor reports the interpreter it runs on, the library
it loaded and the rules it found.
The same program is a language server ( sift lsp ). The findings, the fixes and
the formatting are computed once and delivered either as text on standard
output or as LSP responses, so Emacs through Eglot, Neovim and any other client
of the protocol are told exactly what a pipeline is told.
It ships as one executable and one Emacs package, under the MIT license. The
premise is the ordinary one: a Lisp program is a datum with a read syntax, and
a formatter that treats it as such can be exact and cheap at the same time.
Check, format, lint. sift check prints the patch it would make and exits
1; sift format prints the formatted file; sift lint names the rule that
fired, its severity and its position. The editor and the pipeline receive
these same answers. Every line in that recording is real output, on files
small enough to read in the picture.
Scope and audience
Students of Lisp. Each dialect is read by its own report, so the tool in
front of a learner enforces the conventions of the language being learned
rather than a fourth one invented by a formatter.
Guile and Guix code bases , whose cond clauses are written with square
brackets and whose build files are gexps, want a formatter that agrees with
the tree next door instead of re-deciding it.
Emacs package authors who need the docstring, lexical-binding ,
interactive and provide rules in Flymake and in CI, from one program
rather than three.
Common Lisp projects in which package prefixes, LOOP keyword style and
dangling parentheses are convention, and are preserved rather than
normalised away.
Polyglot Lisp repositories , which get one executable, one configuration
file and one CI step instead of three of each.
Editor and tool authors , who take the findings as data: --format=json ,
--format=sarif , GitHub annotations, or sift lsp .
Lossless rewriting is the whole of the argument, and the rest follows from it:
a diff whose hunks are the change, a fix that replaces one range, a rule that
can be silenced without editing the code it objects to.
Properties and guarantees
Byte-exact preservation. Comments, blank lines, #; datum comments,
#. read-time forms and #<...> objects return exactly as they were read.
Formatting is a fixed point: the second run changes nothing. The suite
asserts preservation and idempotence over every fixture.
The dialect is determined, not assumed. Three dialects, one program:
character literals, read macros, #| ... |# block comments, #; datum
comments, package prefixes, LOOP and docstring conventions follow the
dialect’s own report rather than a compromise. So does a square bracket,
which is a vector in Emacs Lisp and a clause in Scheme, and #{ ... }# ,
which is a symbol and only Guile reads. Guile is the dialect sift is written
in and the one its reader knows most closely; the other two are read from
their specifications.
Three jobs, three commands. Formatting, linting and fixing are separate
by design: format prints, --write writes, lint reports, lint --fix
fixes, and ci asks the formatting question and the lint question in one
pass without touching the tree.
Ninety-two rules, each with its rationale. Every rule has a name, a
stable code ( SIFT012 ), a sentence, the dialects it applies to, an example
and its own test file. sift explain RULE reads the reasoning out of the
program, and doc/rules.org is generated from the rule records, so the
book cannot drift from the code it describes.
A fix that refuses to guess. A rule’s fix replaces exactly one range, and
every fix of a run is discarded if together they would introduce a parse
error. No delimiter is invented and no identifier is renamed.
Suppression is a comment, and it stays where the code is.
;; sift:disable-next-line keyword-arguments switches one rule off for one
line, disable for the rest of the form it sits in, and enable turns it
back on. Suppression is line-oriented and form-scoped by design: an
exception list in a configuration file is a list that no review ever reaches,
and a range comment outlives the code it was written for.
One language server, every editor. sift lsp speaks LSP over standard
input and output: diagnostics, quickfixes and formatting, go to definition
and references for all three dialects – including the names the standard
library and its installed packages define, the documentation an
implementation carries for the ones it compiled in, and the compressed
sources most Emacs installations ship – an outline, completion, inlay hints
that name a call’s arguments, a hover that describes a symbol or the rule
under it, import organization, a file rename that keeps its module in step,
and a second opinion from the dialect’s own compiler when a buffer is saved.
Output for humans, editors and pipelines. The compile-style line that
:make and compilation-mode parse, JSON for editors that want structure,
SARIF 2.1.0 for code scanning, GitHub annotatio

hn.title: Show HN: Reflota – Open-source data recovery for NTFS/FAT disks with phased copy
hn.text:
Reflota
Recuperá archivos de discos, pendrives y tarjetas (NTFS, FAT32, FAT16, FAT12 y exFAT), incluso los que borraste. Gratis, de código abierto y en modo solo lectura.
Cuando Windows dice "el disco no está formateado" , una carpeta no abre o el explorador se cuelga, muchas veces los archivos siguen ahí. Reflota los reconstruye leyendo el disco directamente: en NTFS lee toda la tabla maestra (MFT) y arma el árbol de carpetas con la información que cada archivo guarda de su propia carpeta; en FAT y exFAT lee las carpetas y sigue las cadenas de clusters.
También encuentra archivos borrados y te dice cuántos de ellos siguen recuperables. Y si el disco se formateó o ya no tiene nombres, puede buscar archivos por su contenido , encontrar particiones perdidas y hacer una copia segura de un disco que está fallando.
Estado: beta. Funciona, pero cada disco dañado es distinto. Probalo primero con una copia de lo importante si podés.
Novedades todavía sin probar en discos reales (se verificaron con imágenes de prueba, no con hardware): FAT16/FAT12, búsqueda de RAW de cámara/PSD/RAR, reconstrucción de JPEG fragmentados, buscador por nombre y copia por fases. Si probás alguna con un disco real, contá cómo te fue en Issues .
Descarga
Bajá Reflota.exe desde la sección Releases . No necesita instalación ni Python.
Como el programa no está firmado digitalmente, Windows puede mostrar "Windows protegió su PC" : tocá Más información → Ejecutar de todas formas . Algunos antivirus desconfían de los programas que leen discos de forma directa; el código es abierto y podés compilar el .exe vos mismo (ver más abajo). Junto a cada Release se publica el hash SHA256 para comprobar que la descarga no se corrompió.
Cómo se usa
Abrí Reflota . Aparece la lista de tus discos y unidades.
Tildá lo que querés recuperar, todo en el mismo árbol:
Tildar un disco o una partición → se copia todo .
Entrá en la partición y tildá solo carpetas o archivos → se copia solo eso .
El tamaño total se calcula solo mientras tildás.
Activá Incluir archivos borrados para ver también lo que se borró: aparece en rojo, en su carpeta original, con su estado.
Buscar por nombre (arriba del árbol): escribí parte del nombre ( factura ), un patrón ( *.pdf , foto_??.jpg ) y apretá Enter. Busca sin importar mayúsculas ni acentos, en la partición elegida (o en todas las que ya abriste), incluye lo borrado y muestra los resultados como un grupo nuevo del árbol que se tilda igual que lo demás. Primero abrí la partición (clic en su flecha).
Abajo, elegí la carpeta donde copiar (en otro disco ) y apretá RECUPERAR .
Podés parar cuando quieras y volver a empezar: lo que ya se copió no se repite.
Sobre los permisos de administrador
Windows no deja leer un disco "en crudo" sin permisos de administrador (le pasa a cualquier programa de recuperación). Reflota abre sin pedirlos y los pide recién cuando tocás un disco para leerlo; ahí se reabre con el aviso de Windows. El programa nunca escribe en el disco de origen .
Herramientas (menú «Herramientas»)
Elegí primero un disco o una partición en la lista.
Buscar archivos por contenido. Reconoce los archivos por su forma interna, sin necesitar nombres ni carpetas. Sirve cuando el disco se formateó, la tabla de archivos está destruida o el archivo borrado ya perdió su nombre. Podés buscar solo en el espacio libre (rápido, ideal para lo borrado) o en todo el disco o la partición. Los resultados aparecen en el mismo árbol, agrupados por tipo, y se recuperan igual que lo demás (tildar y RECUPERAR). Detecta: fotos (JPG, PNG, GIF, BMP, WebP, HEIC, TIFF), fotos RAW de cámara (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RW2, PEF, RAF), PSD/PSB de Photoshop, videos (MP4/MOV/3GP, AVI, MKV/WebM), audio (MP3, M4A, WAV), documentos (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, ODT/ODS/ODP, DOC/XLS/PPT, EPUB), comprimidos (ZIP, RAR, 7Z, JAR, APK) y bases de datos SQLite. El largo exacto de cada archivo se calcula leyendo su estructura (no se corta "a ojo"), y los archivos que contienen otros archivos adentro (como una miniatura en una foto) salen enteros. Los nombres originales no se pueden recuperar : salen numerados ( recuperado_00012.jpg ). Los archivos que estaban fragmentados (partidos en pedazos no contiguos) normalmente no se pueden rearmar y pueden salir incompletos o mezclados, salvo las fotos JPEG si tildás Reconstruir fotos JPEG fragmentadas : Reflota decodifica la foto hasta donde deja de ser válida y busca el pedazo que la continúa; solo la entrega si el resultado cierra exacto (todos los bloques de imagen y el final del archivo). Es mucho más lento , funciona con JPEG «baseline» (los de cámaras y celulares; no los progresivos) y puede no lograrlo cuando hay muchos fragmentos o el hueco está lleno de otras fotos parecidas: en ese caso la foto simplemente no aparece (no entrega una foto equivocada a propósito, pero conviene mirar el resultado).
Buscar particiones perdidas. Recorre el disco entero buscando los inicios de particiones NTFS, FAT32, FAT16/12 y exFAT, aunque la tabla de particiones esté borrada y hasta con los sectores de arranque destruidos (usa sus copias de respaldo). Las que encuentra se agregan a la lista. Puede tardar bastante en discos grandes y se puede parar.
Crear imagen del disco (copia segura). Cuando un disco falla, lo mejor es copiarlo una sola vez a un archivo y trabajar sobre esa copia, sin seguir forzando el original. La copia va por fases , como hacen las herramientas de rescate profesionales: primero lee rápido todo lo que se lee bien (saltando las zonas que fallan para no insistir), después recorta los bordes de las zonas dañadas, luego las lee sector por sector y al final reintenta los sectores ilegibles. Así se rescata lo máximo con el mínimo castigo al disco. Los sectores que nunca se pudieron leer quedan en ceros y se anotan en *.malos.txt . El avance se guarda en *.mapa : si se interrumpe (o se corta la luz) se continúa exactamente desde ahí. Después agregás la imagen a la lista y recuperás desde ahí.
Consejos importa

hn.title: Global Microsoft Outage
hn.text:
• Coming back online: Microsoft said it has addressed the underlying issue of a massive outage that affected millions around the world as it continues to restore service. The software giant apologized for disruptions, saying the outage was caused by a technical issue and not a cybersecurity breach.
• Economic ramifications: The cost of lost productivity from the outage could approach at least $7 billion , according to a think-tank estimate.
• What’s been impacted: The outage, which began around noon ET on Thursday, left workers unable to access Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life . AI companies said they were facing issues as well. Banks, governments, health services, railways and courts all reported disruptions across Microsoft products .
• Global disruption: Outage reports “reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour,” according to Downdetector. While some workers scrambled to find workarounds, others expressed relief in a respite from the work grind.

Some railway networks experienced disruption to their customer email services and routing schedules while Australian schools, courts and government services reported disruption.
What caused this? Microsoft said the outage was caused by a “technical issue” rather than any cybersecurity breach . “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.
While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity .
Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:
Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.
Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena , arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA .
Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.
Web development : On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.
Using Hydrogen for on-the-fly 3D coding, Geminisland lets anyone add to a shared voxel island from a single prompt to generate custom structures live on the map that players can walk around and explore in first person. Try the live app .
Paired with our new Gemini front end design skill in Google Antigravity, Hydrogen built an e-commerce storefront in one shot complete with a WebGL2 topographic shader, pinned four-stage scrollytelling, a thermal split-slider, a 3D wireframe spec card, and a live finish configurator. Try the live app and the Gemini front end design skill .

Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang
hn.text:
Save this story
Save this story
Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation , according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset . The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.
Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24.
Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned . In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”
Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data
hn.text: Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo ( https://leeroo.com/ ). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso ( https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso ), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run. The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation. For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions. The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox. We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack. You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs Here’s how it works… Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it. For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject. After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic. kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations. We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results… - Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model ( https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/ ). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model. - ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems ( https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107 ). - AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems ( https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re... ). We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia ( https://leeroopedia.com/ ): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents. If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help! https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso

hn.title: Yang-Mills, OpenAI proof, and the mass gap problem
hn.text:

Yang-Mills, OpenAI proof, and the mass gap problem
Community Article Published
November 13, 2026
Upvote 13
+7
David Louapre dlouapre Follow

A few days ago, OpenAI made an announcement about the existence of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics . It sounds like a physics problem but this is actually the first half of the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem, one of the seven 1-million $ questions from the Clay Institute.
After Navier-Stokes a few weeks ago, my first thought was, OpenAI did it again?
Actually, not quite...yet.
As usual, to share their results with the world, they produced a huge manuscript (1147 pages !) along with a proof verified in Lean, a programming language in which a computer checks every single logical step of a mathematical proof. But Lean is not enough: we need to make sure that what the proof is about is really the problem mathematicians and physicists are interested in . A computer can check that a proof is correct, but not that the definitions written in the code mean what we think they mean.
For this, OpenAI called a special group to examine their proof. And the group just released its first assessment . To understand what is at stake, let me walk you through the Yang-Mills problem, its link to the strong nuclear force, and whether all of this matters for what happens inside particle accelerators.
Quantum Field Theory : our best framework to understand particles
As its name indicates, quantum field theory is about applying the principles of quantum mechanics to fields, like the electromagnetic field. Quantum mechanics is usually well defined when we are dealing with a finite number of degrees of freedom, like a bunch of point particles each having a position and a velocity. But with fields, which have a value at every point of continuous space, things get finicky.
You may have heard about the path integral approach to quantum mechanics, a beautiful idea due to Richard Feynman. The idea involves computing a giant integral over all the trajectories a particle can follow.
It might sound scary, but with a finite number of particles, we have ways to make this rigorous and well defined by taking careful limits. But applying the same idea to fields is complicated.
For a field, the "trajectories" are all the possible configurations of the field in space and time. Schematically, if A denotes our field and S [ A ] S[A] S [ A ] its action (the quantity that encodes the laws of the classical theory), the path integral reads
Z = ∫ D A    e   i S [ A ] / ℏ
Z = \int \mathcal{D}A \; e^{\,i S[A]/\hbar}
Z = ∫ D A e i S [ A ] /ℏ
where the strange symbol D A \mathcal{D}A D A means "integrate over all possible field configurations" (similar to your familiar d x dx d x in ordinary integrals.) Indeed, with fields existing everywhere in space, the field path integral involves an infinite number of integrals (one for each point of space!), and the path integral becomes generally ill-defined: there is no proper mathematical meaning for D A \mathcal{D}A D A , and divergences appear.
Still, that doesn't stop physicists from writing and manipulating them, in particular to define a certain type of objects called correlation functions :
⟨ O ( x )   O ( y ) ⟩ = 1 Z ∫ D A    O ( x )   O ( y )    e   i S [ A ] / ℏ
\langle O(x)\, O(y) \rangle = \frac{1}{Z}\int \mathcal{D}A \; O(x)\, O(y)\; e^{\,i S[A]/\hbar}
⟨ O ( x ) O ( y )⟩ = Z 1 ​ ∫ D A O ( x ) O ( y ) e i S [ A ] /ℏ
where O is some quantity built from the field, at points x and y. These correlation functions essentially represent what we can observe experimentally, say in particle accelerators. And to see how physicists escape the ill-definedness problem, let's have a look at the quantum side of Maxwell's electromagnetism.
Quantum Electrodynamics
Let's start with pure electromagnetism , when no matter is present. This is the easy case, because the nasty path integrals can then be shown to be computable and well defined...But the resulting theory is not very interesting! This is because it only contains photons (the particle associated with electromagnetism), and they don't interact with each other. Pure electromagnetism is a theory of free photons moving in space, and passing past each other as if they were alone.
Now add matter, for instance electrons. We can write the path integral that describes the coupling of electromagnetism and electrons. The theory is supposed to be way more interesting because photons provide in principle a mean for electrons to interact...but this time the big path integral it is not well defined . So the correlation functions are in theory meaningless.
The good news is that physicists found a way around, called the perturbative expansion .
The so-called coupling between electromagnetism and matter (it measures how strongly they interact, and is related to the famous fine-structure constant α ≈ 1 / 137 \alpha \approx 1/137 α ≈ 1/137 ) is weak enough, at least at large distances, that we can formally expand the ill-defined integrals in powers of this coupling, and truncate this expansion to a finite number of terms that we can actually compute. To show you the idea with a simple numerical integral, imagine you had to compute
I ( α ) = ∫ − ∞ + ∞ e − x 2 − α x 4   d x
I(\alpha) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2 - \alpha x^4}\, dx
I ( α ) = ∫ − ∞ + ∞ ​ e − x 2 − α x 4 d x
then you realize that you can expand e − α x 4 e^{- \alpha x^4} e − α x 4 in power series, which you can truncate to get integrals that are easier to compute
I ( α ) ≈ ∫ − ∞ + ∞ e − x 2 ( 1 − α x 4 + α 2 2 x 8 + …   ) d x
I(\alpha) \approx \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2} \left(1 - \alpha x^4 + \frac{\alpha^2}{2} x^8 + \dots\right) dx
I ( α ) ≈ ∫ − ∞ + ∞ ​ e − x 2 ( 1 − α x 4 + 2 α 2 ​ x 8 + … ) d x
With the perturbative approach, each term of the expansion becomes symbolized by one of the famous "Feynman diagrams" that you probably ha

hn.title: Researchers discover rare star system that emits radio signals every 8 minutes
hn.text:
Scientists at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research ( ICRAR ) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun.
The newly discovered system, known as GPM J071507−114153, consists of two stars orbiting each other: a white dwarf — the dense core left behind when a star dies — and a G-type star similar to our own Sun.
It is the first time radio pulses have been detected from a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star. Typically, such pulses are observed in systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars, meaning the discovery breaks new ground.
These types of stellar pairs belong to a broader class of objects known as long-period transients (LPTs), producing radio signals that switch on and off over intervals ranging from minutes to hours. Around a dozen have been detected since the first was discovered by the same ICRAR team in 2021, and astronomers are still working to understand them.
While several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and another star, it has remained unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses.
“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” said lead author and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory , Dr Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. The team processed more than 100 hours of radio data at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre to validate and understand the white dwarf motion.
Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, co-author on the paper, said that the pulses emitted by the white dwarf allowed the team to detect stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to those that create aurorae here on Earth.
“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”
“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”
ICRAR researchers have been at the forefront of discovering these rare systems.
“We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.
After the LPT was located using the radio telescopes, the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star through optical observations.
Both the MWA, led by Curtin University at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia, and MeerKAT , built and operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in the country’s North Cape province, serve as precursors for the SKA telescopes, SKA-Low in Australia and the SKA-Mid in South Africa, respectively.
Dr McSweeney said, “If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.”
This study, ‘ A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion’ , was published in Nature Astronomy.
